items.title: Measles is back in the United States, WHO authorities say
items.snippet: The Pan American Health Organization has determined that the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status, meaning domestic spread of the virus is now significant and sustained.

items.title: 5,000-year-old skulls reveal a disturbing secret of ancient Egypt's first kings
items.snippet: A 5,000-year-old mystery surrounding the tombs of Egypt’s first kings has taken a disturbing turn. Scientists reexamining 46 ancient skulls discovered evidence of potentially fatal head injuries in 18, suggesting that at least 39% of those studied may have been deliberately killed. items.title: Scientists capture electrons making seemingly impossible quantum jumps
items.snippet: Scientists have captured electrons making seemingly impossible jumps across forbidden energy gaps in graphene, with some transitions occurring at a remarkable 100% probability. The breakthrough offers an unprecedented look at quantum behavior and could help unlock a new generation of ultrafast, light-controlled electronics.

items.title: SpaceX's Starship soars into orbit after booster explosion prevents an unprecedented double catch
items.snippet: SpaceX's attempt to recover its entire Starship back at the launch pad was thwarted when the booster fell into the Gulf of Mexico and exploded Friday, but the spacecraft still soared into orbit in its boldest test yet.

items.title: Happy face, angry voice: Human–dog interaction study tracks conflicting cues
items.snippet: Dogs, having lived alongside humans for tens of thousands of years, are keenly tuned in to our emotions. Behavioral experiments, brain studies and even measurements of heart rate all suggest dogs respond differently depending on the emotional expressions they encounter in humans.

items.title: A newly discovered South African dinosaur was a heavyweight even as a youngster
items.snippet: It probably walked on two legs and weighed about 400 kilograms (880 pounds), despite still being a youngster. Meet Nyana rooiwalensis, a newly identified dinosaur species that lived more than 200 million years ago in what is now South Africa.

items.title: Molecular sensor makes invisible traces of mercury easier to see
items.snippet: Mercury contamination presents an obvious challenge: it is invisible. A glass of water or a piece of fruit can seem perfectly normal to the naked eye, even when trace amounts of toxic mercury are present. Detecting such minute levels usually requires specialized laboratory tools and trained experts.

items.title: Fruit fly sleep protein yields peptides that inhibit drug-resistant bacteria in lab tests
items.snippet: Researchers at University of Tsukuba and collaborating institutions have identified short antimicrobial peptides derived from Nemuri, a sleep-inducing protein in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. The research is published in the journal Nature Communications.

items.title: New genetic atlas reveals traces of 10,000 years of sheep breeding
items.snippet: For around 10,000 years, humans have selectively bred sheep for desirable traits. Generation after generation, we have chosen animals for their wool, size and reproductive characteristics and gradually left our mark on their DNA.

items.title: How Chinese brewers refined their booze 5,000 years ago
items.snippet: More than 5,000 years ago, brewers in eastern China appear to have used red mold to make rice alcohol, then strained the drink through cloth. Microscopic residues on ancient pottery show evidence of both the fermentation method and the filtering process to separate the liquid from leftover grain.

items.title: Kindergarten teachers offer cognitive help during outdoor play but fall short on emotional and social support
items.snippet: A study in the International Journal of Innovation and Sustainable Development of teachers' behavior during outdoor play at kindergarten has identified a gap between the support children need and the help educators provide, particularly in emotional and social development.
